questions.question: Why did the Prophet Muhammad recite Surah Qaf regularly every Friday from the pulpit?
options: A. Because it is the shortest surah and easy to memorize
B. To keep the community constantly revisiting its themes of resurrection, accountability, and divine power
C. Because it was the first surah revealed in Mecca
D. To honor the letter Qaf as one of the names of Allah
questions.explanation: The tafsir notes that the Prophet recited Surah Qaf every Friday in his khutba to ensure the community continually revisited its foundational themes of resurrection and accountability. Ibn Kathir cites the hadith from Sahih Muslim narrated by Umm Hisham al-Ansariyya confirming this practice.

questions.question: Imam Tabari held a firm and definitive opinion that the letter Qaf at the opening of this surah refers to a mountain that surrounds the earth.
questions.explanation: Tabari recorded multiple scholarly positions on the letter Qaf, including the mountain interpretation, but he himself preferred the view that these disconnected letters are among the matters whose knowledge belongs to Allah alone. Ibn Kathir in Tafsir al-Quran al-Azim affirmed the same position of scholarly humility before these mysteries.

questions.question: What was the core reason the Meccan disbelievers rejected the Prophet's message according to verse 2?
options: A. They found his arguments logically flawed and demanded further signs
B. They were astonished that a warner came from among themselves, a human they already knew
C. They objected that the message contained no new moral teachings
D. They rejected it because the message was delivered in an unfamiliar dialect
questions.explanation: The tafsir explains that the disbelievers marveled that the warner was 'from among themselves' (minhum) — an ordinary man they knew personally. Their rejection was rooted in arrogance and social pride rather than intellectual objection. The phrase 'this is a strange thing' was their dismissal based on the familiarity of a human being claiming divine selection.

questions.question: Fakhr al-Din al-Razi noted that verse 2 uses 'mundhir' (warner) rather than 'mubashir' (bringer of glad tidings). What reason did he give for this choice?
options: A. Because the Prophet had not yet been given permission to announce Paradise
B. Because the dominant theme being introduced is accountability and resurrection, which calls first for a warning
C. Because the disbelievers specifically requested a warner rather than a bringer of good news
D. Because 'mubashir' was a term reserved exclusively for angels in Quranic usage
questions.explanation: In Mafatih al-Ghayb, Fakhr al-Din al-Razi observes that the Quran's selection of 'mundhir' reflects the context of Surah Qaf: the dominant theme introduced is accountability and resurrection, subjects that naturally call for a warning before a promise of reward.

questions.question: The disbelievers' declaration 'that is a far return' in verse 3 was a sincere expression of intellectual doubt about the mechanics of resurrection.
questions.explanation: According to the tafsir, 'that is a far return' was an expression of mockery and disbelief, not genuine inquiry. The Quran records their words not to validate them but to invite every reader to confront the question seriously. Their stance was reactive and driven by pride rather than honest investigation.

questions.question: Wahbah al-Zuhayli noted that modern forensic science illustrates the Quranic claim in verse 4. What does that verse assert?
options: A. That the Quran contains scientific details that were unknown until the modern era
B. That Allah's knowledge of what the earth takes from every human body makes resurrection entirely possible
C. That the angels record deeds using methods resembling forensic analysis
D. That the Preserved Tablet functions like a comprehensive genetic database
questions.explanation: In Al-Tafsir al-Munir, Wahbah al-Zuhayli argues that if humans with limited forensic tools can reconstruct so much from microscopic bone fragments, this glimpse of human knowledge illustrates the divine knowledge verse 4 describes: Allah knows precisely what the earth diminishes of every person, making the materialist objection to resurrection collapse.

questions.question: In verse 6 Allah invites humanity to observe the sky and notice it has no 'furuj.' What does this word mean, and what does it support?
options: A. The sky has no permanent clouds, proving Allah alone controls weather patterns
B. The sky has no rifts or cracks, demonstrating seamless divine craftsmanship that supports the case for resurrection
C. The sky has no visible boundary, proving the cosmos is infinite by divine will
D. The sky has no audible sound, proving Allah's creation operates without disturbance
questions.explanation: The tafsir explains that 'furuj' means rifts, cracks, or fissures. The verse argues that if Allah built and sustains the vast heavens without any defect, He is more than capable of raising the dead. Imam al-Qurtubi notes this as an argument (dalil) for omnipotence drawn from visible creation.

questions.question: Imam al-Qurtubi held that verse 6's call to look at the sky contains an implicit command to engage in deep contemplation (tadabbur) of creation, and that such reflection is among the highest acts of intellectual worship.
questions.explanation: In Al-Jami li-Ahkam al-Quran, Imam al-Qurtubi notes that the interrogative 'Have they not looked?' carries an implicit command to engage in tadabbur, and he affirms that contemplation of creation is among the highest acts of intellectual worship because it leads the mind to recognize the power and majesty of the Creator.

questions.question: What was the main scholarly disagreement about the 'companions of the well' (Ashab al-Rass) mentioned in verse 12?
options: A. Whether they lived before or after the people of Noah
B. Whether their prophet was Hud or Shu'ayb
C. Their precise historical identity, with some identifying them as a remnant of Thamud and others as a distinct community
D. Whether the well was a physical landmark or a metaphor for spiritual decline
questions.explanation: As recorded by Imam Tabari in Jami al-Bayan, classical scholars differed on who the Ashab al-Rass were. Some held they were a surviving remnant of Thamud; others, including Qatada, identified them as a distinct Arab community who threw their prophet into an actual well. Ibn Kathir acknowledged this uncertainty while affirming that the theological lesson is identical regardless of their specific identity.

questions.question: Sayyid Qutb argued in Fi Zilal al-Quran that the rapid listing of destroyed nations such as Ad, Pharaoh, and the brothers of Lut is purely a history lesson with no direct relevance to later generations.
questions.explanation: In Fi Zilal al-Quran, Sayyid Qutb explicitly argues the opposite: the enumeration of destroyed nations is a confrontation with cosmic reality, not history for academic interest. He describes it as revealing the permanent operating law of the universe — that arrogance and rejection of divine guidance lead to ruin — and applies this to every age including the modern world.

questions.question: What spiritual quality does verse 16's declaration 'We are closer to him than his jugular vein' aim to cultivate in the believer?
options: A. Asceticism, prompting withdrawal from worldly concerns
B. Muraqabah, the constant consciousness that Allah witnesses every thought, intention, and movement
C. Isolation in worship and avoidance of all social interaction
D. Gratitude, since the verse focuses on Allah's closeness as a sign of His generosity
questions.explanation: The tafsir explains that the image of the jugular vein conveys an intimacy beyond anything physical, and its practical lesson is muraqabah — the awareness that Allah witnesses every thought and intention. This awareness should inspire not fear alone but a sense of being accompanied and accountable at every moment, transforming the believer's private life and inner sincerity.

questions.question: What mercy embedded in the system of the two recording angels did Imam Tabari record from scholars of the early generations regarding verse 17?
options: A. The right angel records only good deeds and bad deeds are never written at all
B. The right angel may hold the recording of a sin for a period to allow repentance before it is permanently entered
C. Both angels rest on Fridays so deeds on that day are not recorded
D. The angels only begin recording after a person reaches the age of forty
questions.explanation: In Jami al-Bayan, Imam Tabari cites narrations from scholars of the Salaf indicating that when a person commits a sin, the angel of the right may hold the recording — some reports say for six or seven hours — to allow the person to repent before the act is permanently entered. This highlights the divine mercy woven into the system of angelic accountability.

questions.question: Verse 18 of Surah Qaf teaches that only sinful or harmful words are recorded by the watching angel, while mundane statements are excluded from the record.
questions.explanation: The tafsir is explicit that verse 18 covers every word without exception. Imam Tabari records in Jami al-Bayan that the scholarly consensus interprets 'ma yalfizu min qawlin' as any utterance at all, including purely mundane statements, with judgment accounting for the varying nature and impact of each word.

questions.question: Sheikh Muhammad al-Sharawi offered a distinctive insight on why verse 33 describes fearing 'al-Rahman' (the Most Merciful) rather than a more fearsome divine name. What was his point?
options: A. That fear and mercy are contradictory, so the verse must be read as purely metaphorical
B. That fearing al-Rahman means one fears being deprived of His mercy, a deeper awareness than merely fearing punishment
C. That al-Rahman is used here because the verse was addressed specifically to the women of Mecca
D. That al-Rahman is the easiest divine name for ordinary people to understand and relate to
questions.explanation: In his tafsir commentary, Sheikh Muhammad al-Sharawi pointed out that the deliberate choice of the name al-Rahman signals that the person who truly understands Allah's mercy fears being deprived of it far more than they fear punishment alone. The greatest possible loss is losing closeness to the One who is infinitely generous and merciful, making this the highest form of taqwa described in verse 33.

questions.question: The closing verse of Surah Qaf commands the Prophet to 'remind with the Quran whoever fears My warning.' What principle about Islamic guidance does this teach?
options: A. That the Quran should only be recited to scholars and the religiously trained
B. That political authority must be established before the Quran can serve as a reminder
C. That the Quran itself is the sufficient instrument of guidance, offered through invitation rather than compulsion, to those with receptive hearts
D. That warnings of divine punishment are more effective than promises of reward in guiding people
questions.explanation: The tafsir explains that this final verse closes on three interlocking notes: Allah is fully aware of what deniers say, the Prophet is not a compeller (jabbar), and the Quran is the tool of reminder for those who fear divine accountability. True faith cannot be forced but must come through invitation and receptivity. Al-Qurtubi connects this to the broader Quranic principle 'there is no compulsion in religion' (2:256).
